- **Derive** new features: bin a continuous column and pull the parts out of a date. *(Apply)*

## Why This Matters

In L10 you *explored* the Ames homes -- read their distributions, compared neighborhoods by eye. An
algorithm cannot do any of that with the table as it sits. It cannot consume `Neighborhood = "CollgCr"`;
it cannot tell that a `YearBuilt` of 2003 means "almost new"; and if you hand it `LotArea` (in the ten
thousands) next to `FullBath` (zero to three), it will treat the lot size as thousands of times more
important purely because the numbers are bigger.

Between a tidy table you can *read* and a matrix an algorithm can *use* sits one job: **feature
engineering** -- deciding what to measure and putting every measurement into comparable numbers. A line
widely attributed to the machine-learning researcher Andrew Ng puts it bluntly: *"Applied machine learning
is basically feature engineering."* Units I--III taught you to store, fetch, and explore data. Unit IV is
about *mining information* from it, and that starts here, by building the columns the rest of the unit will
mine.

## What Is a Feature?

> **Analogy:** a doctor cannot put "the patient" into a formula. She measures things *about* the patient --
> temperature, blood pressure, heart rate -- and works with those numbers. The measurements are the
> features; the patient is the raw data.

A **feature** is a measurable property of an observation, expressed as a number (or something convertible
to one). Stack them in a table -- one row per observation, one column per feature -- and you have a
**feature matrix**, conventionally called `X`:

| | GrLivArea | age | style_2Story | nb_CollgCr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| house 1 | 1710 | 7 | 1 | 1 |
| house 2 | 1262 | 34 | 0 | 0 |
| house 3 | 1786 | 9 | 1 | 1 |

This is exactly the tidy-table shape from Unit III, with one new demand: **every column must end up
numeric**. L07's variable taxonomy still governs what each column *means* -- continuous, discrete,
ordinal, nominal -- but algorithms consume numbers, so every raw input (a category name, a year, a date,
a sentence) needs a defined path into `X`. The four paths this lesson covers, by raw type:

- **Nominal category** (`HouseStyle`, `Neighborhood`) -- one-hot encode.
- **Numeric on an odd scale** (`LotArea`, `GrLivArea`) -- standardize or min-max.
- **Continuous you want as groups** (`YearBuilt`) -- bin it.
- **A date or year** -- derive parts (age, month, day-of-week).

Sometimes the work is already done: `OverallQual` arrives as an integer 1--10 that *encodes its own order*
-- it is a usable feature as-is, and one-hot encoding it would throw the ordering away.

## Encoding Categoricals: One-Hot

An algorithm cannot read `"2Story"`. The temptation is to map the categories to `1, 2, 3, ...` -- but that
invents an order and a spacing that are not real (`SLvl` is not "three times" `1Story`). **One-hot
encoding** avoids the lie: one new 0/1 column per category value, exactly one of them hot per row.

| HouseStyle | | style_1Story | style_2Story | style_SLvl |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2Story | becomes | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 1Story | | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| SLvl | | 0 | 0 | 1 |

In pandas it is one call -- `pd.get_dummies(df["HouseStyle"], prefix="style", dtype=int)`. On the real
Ames data, `HouseStyle` has **8** distinct values (the real list includes half-story variants like
`1.5Fin`, not just the three shown above), so it expands into **8** clean 0/1 columns. So far so good.

::: {.callout-warning title="When one-hot explodes"}
One column per value is fine for `HouseStyle` (8 values). It is a disaster for high-cardinality columns.
`Neighborhood` has **25** values -- one-hot turns one column into **25**, most of them almost all zeros.
Push that to a real ID column (customer IDs, product codes, with thousands of values) and the matrix gains
thousands of nearly-empty columns. High-cardinality categoricals need other strategies -- the simplest is
to group the rare values into a single `"Other"` bucket before encoding.
:::

## Scaling Numerics: Putting Columns on One Footing

Raw numeric columns live on wildly different scales. In Ames, `LotArea` averages about **10,517** while
`FullBath` ranges **0--3**. Many core algorithms -- anything that measures **distance** between rows
(clustering, nearest neighbors, PCA in L20) or follows a **gradient** -- read a bigger spread as "more
important." Left raw, `LotArea` would dominate `FullBath` for no reason but its units. **Scaling** removes
that accident.

Two standard moves:

**Standardization (z-score)** -- recenter to mean 0, rescale to standard deviation 1:

$$
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

In pandas that is `(x - x.mean()) / x.std(ddof=0)`. Standardize Ames `GrLivArea` and the column comes out
with **mean 0.0** and **std 1.0**; its first three values become `0.3703, -0.4825, 0.515` -- a home a
third of a standard deviation above average, one half a deviation below, one half above. The numbers are
now comparable across columns.

**Min-max normalization** -- squeeze the column into the range `[0, 1]`:

$$
x' = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}
$$

The same `GrLivArea` then runs from exactly **0.0** (the smallest home) to **1.0** (the largest). Use
min-max when you want a bounded range; use standardization when the spread (in standard deviations) is what
matters. Either way you compute the recipe **once** and apply the *same* recipe everywhere -- which is
precisely what scikit-learn's transformers do:

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(df[["GrLivArea"]])   # same z-scores: 0.3703, -0.4825, 0.515
```

`fit` learns the mean and std from the data; `transform` applies them. This **fit/transform** pattern is
the backbone of the rest of the unit -- you will meet it again for feature selection (L13) and for the
models in L14--L15.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Deep Dive: ddof, and why hand-rolled and library z-scores can differ (optional)"}
`StandardScaler` divides by the **population** standard deviation (`ddof=0`). Pandas' `.std()` defaults to
the **sample** standard deviation (`ddof=1`, dividing by `n-1`). For `n = 1460` the two differ by about
0.03% -- invisible until the last decimal -- but it is why a from-scratch z-score can disagree with a
library one in the final digits. We pass `ddof=0` above so the pandas formula and `StandardScaler` agree
exactly. The choice never matters for the *purpose* of scaling; it matters only when you compare two
implementations digit for digit.
:::

## Binning and Derived Features

Not every useful feature is a copy of a raw column. Two everyday moves invent new ones.

**Binning (discretization)** turns a continuous column into ordered groups. `pd.cut` slices on
fixed-width edges; `pd.qcut` slices on quantiles so each group holds about the same number of rows. Cut
`YearBuilt` into decades and you trade 112 distinct build years for a handful of human-meaningful eras --
the "built in the 2000s" group alone holds **364** of the 1,460 homes. Binning can also tame outliers and
expose a non-straight-line pattern, at the cost of throwing away within-bin detail.

**Derived features** combine or transform columns into something more informative than either part:

- A **date or year** rarely helps as a raw number; its *parts* do. From `YearBuilt`, derive
  `age = 2010 - YearBuilt` (2010 is the year the data was collected): now the column means "how old,"
  which is what actually drives price. On the Ames homes that `age` averages about **38.7** years and runs
  from **0** to **138**.
- A true **timestamp** carries even more. From a `datetime`, `pandas` pulls the parts directly:

| ts | .dt.year | .dt.month | .dt.dayofweek | is_weekend |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021-03-15 | 2021 | 3 | 0 | False |
| 2021-07-04 | 2021 | 7 | 6 | True |
| 2021-12-25 | 2021 | 12 | 5 | True |

  `dayofweek` runs Monday `0` to Sunday `6`, so `dayofweek >= 5` flags a weekend -- one line that often
  carries more signal than the raw date ever could.

- **Ratios and differences** that encode domain insight: `rooms_per_floor`, `lot-to-living-area`. A good
  derived feature packs knowledge the algorithm would otherwise have to rediscover.

## What Makes a Feature Useful

Engineering features is easy; engineering *good* ones is the skill. Four quick tests:

1. **Informative** -- it actually varies with what you care about. A column that is the same for every row
   teaches nothing.
2. **Not redundant** -- it adds something the other features do not already carry. (L13 makes "redundant"
   precise and removes it.)
3. **Computable when you need it** -- you can produce its value for a *new* observation at the moment you
   must act, not only in hindsight.
4. **It does not leak the label.** This is the one that bites. A feature that secretly encodes the answer
   gives perfect results in testing and fails completely in the wild.

> **The leak test:** if you could only compute this feature *because you already know the outcome*, it is a
> leak. `price_per_sqft` built from `SalePrice` predicts `SalePrice` flawlessly and is useless -- it *is*
> the target in disguise. `rooms_per_floor` is fine: you can measure it for a house that has not sold.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Scaling with statistics from the whole dataset before splitting.** The mean and std must be learned
  from training data only; learning them from data you will later test on leaks information. (You will set
  up proper splits in L15.)
- **One-hot on a high-cardinality column.** Thousands of near-empty columns slow everything and help
  nothing. Group rare values first.
- **Binning away the signal.** Too few bins erase a real trend; bins drawn to flatter the story are a
  classic way to mislead. Bin for a reason, and keep the raw column when in doubt.
- **Inventing a feature that encodes the label.** The single most common cause of a model that looks
  perfect in the notebook and collapses in production. Always ask: could I compute this *before* I knew the
  answer?

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Isn't this just data cleaning from Unit I?"** -- Cleaning makes the data *correct* (fix types, fill
missing values); feature engineering makes it *useful* (invent the columns worth measuring). You clean
first, then engineer. They are different jobs with different goals.

**"Do modern AI models make feature engineering obsolete?"** -- They automate part of it: deep models
*learn* representations instead of being handed engineered ones. But most professional data work is
tabular, modest in size, and must be explained on demand -- and there, engineered features still dominate.
Even cutting-edge pipelines begin with a human deciding what raw signal is worth measuring. The judgment
this lesson teaches does not expire with the tooling.

## Cheat-sheet

| Raw situation | Feature move | Call |
|---|---|---|
| Nominal category, few values | one-hot encode | `pd.get_dummies(..., dtype=int)` |
| Nominal category, hundreds of values | group rare values, then encode | `value_counts` + mapping |
| Already an ordered number | leave it alone | -- (it is a feature) |
| Numeric on an odd scale | standardize | `StandardScaler` / `(x-mean)/std` |
| Numeric, want a bounded range | min-max | `(x-min)/(max-min)` |
| Continuous you want as groups | bin it | `pd.cut` (width) / `pd.qcut` (count) |
| A year or date | derive parts (age, month, weekday) | `2010 - year`, `.dt.*` |
| Two columns imply a better one | derive it (ratio, difference) | plain pandas |
